segments.text: Here's an experiment you can do with your lunch. Take a plain cracker, and keep chewing. Don't swallow. Give it a minute or so… and it starts to taste sweet.

segments.text: But you didn't add any sugar. So where's that sweetness coming from?

segments.text: A molecule in your saliva, doing something that would otherwise take millions of years.

segments.text: Crackers are packed with starch. Zoom right in, and starch is a chain: hundreds, even thousands, of glucose molecules, linked end to end. Glucose is a sugar, but locked up in a chain like this, it doesn't taste sweet.

segments.text: And those links are tough. Left alone in water, a single link would take millions of years to break.

segments.text: Enter amylase: an enzyme in your saliva. It snips starch into smaller sugars, like maltose, which is just two glucose units joined together. And maltose does taste sweet.

segments.text: That's what an enzyme is: a biological catalyst. It speeds up a reaction without being used up. And nearly every reaction in your body has one. Without enzymes, the chemistry that keeps you alive would be far too slow. Nearly all enzymes are proteins, long chains of amino acids folded into a precise shape. And that shape is everything.

Without enzymes, the chemistry that keeps you alive would be far too slow. Nearly all enzymes are proteins, long chains of amino acids folded into a precise shape. And that shape is everything.

segments.text: Every enzyme has a small pocket called the active site. The molecule it works on, the substrate, fits inside, forming an enzyme–substrate complex. Held there, a bond becomes much easier to break. Snap. The products leave, and the active site is free for the next one.
segments.ttsText: Every enzyme has a small pocket called the active site. The molecule it works on, the substrate, fits inside, forming an enzyme substrate complex. Held there, a bond becomes much easier to break. Snap. The products leave, and the active site is free for the next one.

segments.text: The active site's shape is complementary to the substrate: they fit together like a lock and a key. That's why enzymes are so specific. Amylase can't even break down cellulose, in paper, though that's a chain of glucose too. Its links are joined differently, so it just doesn't fit.

segments.text: Lock and key is a brilliant model, but it is a simplification. Real enzymes aren't rigid. As the substrate binds, the active site moulds itself around it. That more accurate picture is called induced fit. For GCSE and IGCSE, lock and key is the model to use. Just remember: it's a model, not a photograph.

segments.text: Which brings us to myth number one: that enzymes get used up. They don't. After each reaction, the enzyme is unchanged, ready to go again, and again. And some are astonishingly fast. One molecule of catalase, from your liver, can break down millions of molecules of hydrogen peroxide a second.

And some are astonishingly fast. One molecule of catalase, from your liver, can break down millions of molecules of hydrogen peroxide a second.

segments.text: Enzymes don't last forever: your cells replace old ones. But the reaction itself never uses them up.

segments.text: Now, temperature. Molecules are always jiggling around. Heat them up, and they move faster. Enzymes and substrates bump into each other more often, and with more energy. More successful collisions means more reactions every second. Up to a point, warmer means faster. For many enzymes in your body, that peak, the optimum, is around 37 degrees: body temperature.

segments.text: So what if we keep turning up the heat? Fifty degrees. Sixty. Seventy. Does it just keep getting faster?

segments.text: Here's what actually happens. The rate crashes, and it doesn't recover.

segments.text: An enzyme's shape is held together by lots of weak bonds. Too much heat, and it vibrates so violently that those bonds break. The chain unravels, the active site loses its shape, and the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme has been denatured.

segments.text: It's the same kind of change that turns egg white solid in a hot pan, and, like a cooked egg, cooling it down usually doesn't undo it.

segments.text: Cold is different: it just slows enzymes down. Warm them up, and they recover.

segments.text: And that's myth number two: that heat "kills" enzymes. Enzymes were never alive. An enzyme is a molecule, a very clever one, but it can't die. It's denatured: its active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits. In an exam, that's the answer that gets the marks.

segments.text: pH can do this too. Too acidic, or too alkaline, and the bonds holding the active site in shape are disrupted. Go far enough, and the enzyme is denatured. So every enzyme has an optimum pH. Amylase, in your mouth, works best close to neutral, around pH 7. Your stomach is strongly acidic, often around pH 2, and pepsin, the enzyme that digests protein there, works best right around that. Different enzymes, tuned to different places.

Your stomach is strongly acidic, often around P H 2, and pepsin, the enzyme that digests protein there, works best right around that. Different enzymes, tuned to different places.

segments.text: So, back to that cracker. As you chew, amylase meets the starch. The chains fit its active site, and it snips them into maltose, over and over, without being used up. Your mouth is about 37 degrees and close to neutral: just right. Links that would last millions of years on their own are broken while you chew. That sweetness is enzymes at work, in real time.
